1.title: The Word in the Beginning
1.context: John opens his Gospel with the opening words of Genesis, 'In the beginning,' and introduces Jesus first as the Word, with God before anything was made. This prologue (1:1-18) is the evangelist's own overture; the story itself begins at verse 19.
1.question: What does it change for you to meet Jesus first as the eternal Word, before you meet him as a man in Galilee?

1.title: The Witness Who Was Not the Light
1.context: John the Baptist is introduced as a witness, a role word this Gospel uses constantly: testimony, courts, and verdicts shape its whole telling. The Baptist's errand is deliberately limited; he points, he does not shine.
1.question: Where has God used a witness, someone who simply pointed, in your own coming to faith?

1.title: His Own Did Not Receive Him
1.context: The prologue compresses the whole Gospel into a few lines: made through him, not recognized by the world, refused by his own, and a right given to those who receive him, to become children of God by a birth God works.
1.question: What do you make of the idea that becoming a child of God is a birth received, not a status achieved?

1.title: The Word Became Flesh
1.context: The Greek word for 'made his dwelling' is literally 'tabernacled,' echoing the tent where God's glory lived among Israel in the wilderness. John says that glory was seen in flesh, full of grace and truth.
1.question: How does it affect your reading of Jesus to know his first followers described him as God's glory living in a body?

1.title: Grace and Truth Came Through Jesus Christ
1.context: The name Jesus Christ appears only at the very end of the prologue, verse 17. 'Grace upon grace' pictures one gift arriving in place of another, wave after wave, and verse 18 claims the unseen God has been made known by the Son at his side.
1.question: Which wave of grace, one gift after another, are you living on right now?

2.title: Who Are You?
2.context: The delegation from Jerusalem works through Israel's expectations: the Christ, Elijah returned (Malachi 4:5), and the Prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). John's three refusals clear the stage of every wrong candidate.
2.question: When people press you to define yourself, what can you learn from how plainly John says what he is not?

2.title: A Voice in the Wilderness
2.context: John answers with Isaiah 40:3, a voice preparing the Lord's way. The Pharisees' question about his authority to baptize was a real legal question; baptism of Jews, not just converts, was unusual and drew official attention.
2.question: What would it look like for your life to be a voice that prepares the way for someone greater?

2.title: One You Do Not Know
2.context: Untying a sandal was the work of the lowliest servant, a task Jewish tradition said even a disciple need not do for his teacher. Bethany beyond the Jordan sat on the east bank, where John's baptizing crowds gathered.
2.question: John says the great One is already standing unnoticed in the crowd. Where might God already be present in a place you have overlooked?

2.title: The Lamb of God
2.context: This is the first title John gives Jesus in public. Lambs in Israel's story carry the Passover lamb, the daily temple offerings, and Isaiah's suffering servant, 'like a lamb to the slaughter.' John ties the title to the sin of the world, not Israel only.
2.question: Why do you think John's Gospel introduces Jesus with a title about dying, rather than a title about ruling?

2.title: I Saw the Spirit Rest on Him
2.context: John's Gospel never narrates Jesus' baptism as an event; it gives the Baptist's testimony about it instead. The sign agreed in advance was the Spirit descending and remaining, the mark of the one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit.
2.question: John believed because he saw the sign God promised him. What has God shown you that settled something for you?

3.title: Come and See
3.context: 'Come and see' is this Gospel's recurring invitation, repeated by Philip to Nathanael and echoed by the Samaritan woman ('Come, see a man'). The tenth hour is about 4 p.m. by the usual reckoning; John remembers the hour the way people remember beginnings.
3.question: Who first said 'come and see' to you, and what did you find when you came?

3.title: We Have Found the Messiah
3.context: Messiah is Hebrew for 'anointed one'; John translates it for his readers as Christ, its Greek equivalent. Cephas is Aramaic for rock, Peter in Greek. Jesus renames Simon at first sight, before Simon has done anything at all.
3.question: Andrew's first act as a follower was to fetch his brother. Who is one person you could bring, simply by telling them what you have found?

3.title: Can Anything Good Come from Nazareth?
3.context: Nazareth was a small village that appears nowhere in the Old Testament, which fed Nathanael's skepticism. Philip does not debate him; he repeats Jesus' own invitation, come and see, and lets the meeting do the arguing.
3.question: How do you respond when faith makes sense to you but sounds unlikely to someone you respect?

3.title: Under the Fig Tree
3.context: Fig trees gave shade for study and prayer, and Nathanael's private moment under one becomes the proof that undoes him. Jesus' promise in verse 51 echoes Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28), with the Son of Man in the place of the ladder between heaven and earth.
3.question: Nathanael moved from skepticism to confession in one conversation. What has Jesus seen about your life that no one else could have known?

4.title: They Have No More Wine
4.context: Weddings in a Galilean village could feast for days, and running out of wine was a lasting shame for the groom's family. Cana was a short walk from Nazareth; Jesus' mother was already there when he and his disciples arrived as invited guests.
4.question: Mary states the problem and leaves it with Jesus. What need in front of you right now needs stating that simply?

4.title: My Hour Has Not Yet Come
4.context: 'My hour' is John's name for the appointed time of Jesus' death and glory, sounded here for the first time (2:4) and not arriving until chapter 12. His mother's instruction to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you,' is her only recorded command in this Gospel.
4.question: Where are you being asked to trust God's timing when the hour has clearly not yet come?

4.title: Filled to the Brim
4.context: The six stone jars held water for Jewish purification washing; stone, unlike clay, was considered resistant to ritual impurity. Six jars at twenty to thirty gallons each means the servants hauled well over a hundred gallons on an instruction that made no sense yet.
4.question: The servants obeyed an order whose point they could not see. What instruction are you in the middle of obeying right now?

4.title: You Have Saved the Fine Wine Until Now
4.context: Banquet custom served the best wine first, while palates were fresh. John makes a point of who knew the secret: not the master of the banquet, not the bridegroom who got the credit, but the servants who had drawn the water.
4.question: The servants knew more than the master of the feast. What have you seen of God's work precisely because you were serving in the background?

4.title: The First of His Signs
4.context: John calls Jesus' miracles 'signs,' acts that point beyond themselves, and numbers them: this is the first (2:11); the healing of the official's son is the second (4:54). Capernaum, down by the lake, becomes the base for what follows.
4.question: John says the disciples believed because they saw his glory in this sign. What have you seen that moved you from hearing about Jesus to trusting him?

5.title: Men Selling Cattle, Sheep, and Doves
5.context: The temple courts served Passover pilgrims who could not bring animals from home and needed temple currency for the half-shekel tax. John places this clearing at the start of Jesus' ministry; Matthew, Mark, and Luke place theirs in his final week, and John intends his placement.
5.question: What crowded, noisy arrangements in your own worship might Jesus walk into with clear eyes?

5.title: He Made a Whip Out of Cords
5.context: The whip is made, not found; John shows Jesus surveying the scene and acting deliberately. 'My Father's house' is the claim beneath the act; the boy Jesus had used the same phrase in the temple in Luke's account (Luke 2:49).
5.question: Jesus calls the temple his Father's house. Where does zeal for God's house show up in your life, and what does it cost?

5.title: Zeal for Your House Will Consume Me
5.context: The disciples' memory reaches Psalm 69:9, a psalm of a righteous sufferer. The authorities' demand for a sign is the legal question of the book: by what authority does a Galilean carpenter disrupt the temple trade at Passover?
5.question: The disciples understood this day through Scripture remembered later. What have you only understood about God long after the event?

5.title: Destroy This Temple
5.context: Herod's temple complex had been under construction for forty-six years by this point and would not be finished for decades more. The saying about destroying the temple and raising it in three days echoes through Jesus' trial in the other Gospels (Matthew 26:61).
5.question: Jesus answered with a riddle that only the resurrection solved. How do you hold onto words of Jesus you do not yet understand?

5.title: He Knew What Was in a Man
5.context: John steps in twice as narrator here: the temple was his body (v. 21), and Jesus did not entrust himself to the Jerusalem believers (vv. 24-25). The chapter sets up the night visitor of chapter 3, one of the impressed Jerusalem establishment.
5.question: John distinguishes believing in Jesus from Jesus trusting the believers. What does a faith Jesus could entrust himself to look like?

6.title: He Came to Jesus at Night
6.context: Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. His 'we know' speaks for colleagues who had seen the Passover signs. John will bring him back twice more (7:50; 19:39), each time a step further into the open.
6.question: Nicodemus came at night with a conclusion but not yet faith. When have you approached Jesus carefully, after dark, so to speak?

6.title: Born of Water and the Spirit
6.context: The Greek word for 'again' (anothen) can also mean 'from above,' which may be why Nicodemus hears only the earthly sense. The wind in verse 8 plays on one Greek and Hebrew word (pneuma, ruach) that means wind, breath, and Spirit alike.
6.question: Jesus compares the Spirit to wind you can hear but not control. Where have you heard its sound in your life without being able to trace its path?

6.title: You Are Israel's Teacher
6.context: Ezekiel 36 promised Israel a new heart and God's Spirit within, which is why Jesus expects the teacher of Israel to recognize new birth. Verse 13's claim is unique to this Gospel: no one has ascended to report on heaven except the one who descended.
6.question: Nicodemus's learning could not get him to the new birth. What has Jesus taught you that your own knowledge could not reach?

6.title: God So Loved the World
6.context: The bronze snake is Numbers 21: Israel, bitten and dying, lived by looking at the serpent Moses lifted on a pole. John 3:16 follows directly from it: the lifting up of the Son is the looking point for the world. The Gospel does not mark whether these words are Jesus' speech or the evangelist's reflection.
6.question: John 3:16 says the motive of the gift was love for the world. How does that motive shape the way you think about people far from God?

6.title: Men Loved the Darkness
6.context: The verdict (Greek krisis, also 'judgment') in John's Gospel is often self-executing: light arrives, and people's loves decide. Coming into the light, verse 21 says, is what 'practicing the truth' looks like, so deeds can be seen as God's work.
6.question: Where is the light unwelcome in your life at the moment, and what would coming into it require?

7.title: John Had Not Yet Been Thrown into Prison
7.context: John's Gospel orders events the others compress: Jesus' early Judean ministry overlaps the Baptist's final free months. Aenon near Salim was chosen for plentiful water, a practical note from a baptizer's eye.
7.question: Two fruitful ministries ran side by side in one countryside. How do you handle seasons when God's work through others grows beside your own?

7.title: Everyone Is Going to Him
7.context: The complaint arrives dressed as an argument about ceremonial washing, which suggests John's disciples were defending their distinctives. Their report is factually true and spiritually tone-deaf: everyone was going to him.
7.question: When has loyalty made you see someone else's fruitfulness as your loss?

7.title: Only What Is Given Him from Heaven
7.context: John's answer treats ministry as a gift with edges, received, not seized. His self-testimony in verse 28 points the court back to chapter 1: he had already said, publicly, that he was not the Christ.
7.question: What has been 'given you from heaven,' and where are its edges that you need to accept?

7.title: The Friend of the Bridegroom
7.context: In a Jewish wedding the bridegroom's friend arranged the match and stood guard at the door; hearing the bridegroom's voice meant his work was done and the joy was not his to keep. Verse 30 may be the most quoted sentence ever spoken about ministry.
7.question: Whose increase would complete your joy rather than threaten it?

7.title: Whoever Believes in the Son Has Eternal Life
7.context: The chapter closes with testimony in the voice of John the Baptist continuing or the evangelist reflecting; the Greek marks no seam, and the Gospel leaves it unmarked. Verse 36's fork, believe or reject, is the chapter's last word.
7.question: John places eternal life in the present tense, 'has eternal life.' What difference does that tense make to you today?

8.title: He Had to Pass Through Samaria
8.context: Jews traveling between Judea and Galilee often detoured around Samaria, whose people were despised as half-foreign worshipers of the same God. Sychar sat near ancient Shechem, below Mount Gerizim, the Samaritans' holy mountain. The sixth hour is noon.
8.question: Jesus sat down tired at a well and broke the rules of the map to be there. Where has obedience taken you through country others walk around?

8.title: If You Knew the Gift of God
8.context: 'Living water' in ordinary speech meant running water, a stream rather than a cistern; the woman hears it that way first, as the pattern of this Gospel's dialogues requires. The gift of God and the identity of the asker are the two things Jesus says she lacks.
8.question: Jesus offers before he explains. What gift of God have you received ahead of understanding it?

8.title: Are You Greater Than Our Father Jacob?
8.context: Jacob's well is over a hundred feet deep and still exists at Shechem. The woman measures Jesus against the patriarch who dug it; his answer promises water that becomes a spring inside the drinker, 'springing up to eternal life.'
8.question: Earthly water must be fetched daily; Jesus promises an inner spring. Where are you still making daily trips to a well that leaves you thirsty?

8.title: Go, Call Your Husband
8.context: The request for the living water is answered with the one command that touches her hidden life. Nothing in the text suggests mockery in Jesus' reply; his 'you have spoken truthfully' receives her honesty before it exposes her history.
8.question: Jesus moves a conversation from water to the truth of a life without changing tone. What truth about your life is he gently naming?

8.title: I Who Speak to You Am He
8.context: Mount Gerizim, visible from the well, held the Samaritan temple, destroyed by the Jews a century and a half earlier. Jesus declares worship unbound from both mountains, 'in spirit and in truth,' then says the words 'I am' to a Samaritan woman before he says them anywhere in Jerusalem.
8.question: The first person to hear Jesus call himself the Messiah outright is this woman. What does that tell you about who he chooses to tell?

9.title: She Left Her Water Jar
9.context: The disciples' surprise is recorded without rebuke, and their unasked questions ('What do you want from her?') stay in the text. The woman's testimony repeats the Baptist's pattern in miniature: he told me everything I ever did; could this be the Christ?
9.question: What errand, jar, or plan might you need to leave behind mid-task because you have met Jesus?

9.title: I Have Food You Know Nothing About
9.context: The disciples repeat the woman's literalism with the food, showing the dialogue pattern of this Gospel: a saying, a misunderstanding, then the deepening. His food, doing the will of the One who sent him, echoes the charge he will repeat through the farewell discourse.
9.question: What work of obedience has fed you in a way rest and meals could not?

9.title: Lift Up Your Eyes and Look at the Fields
9.context: 'Four months until the harvest' was likely a local proverb about waiting. The sower and reaper rejoicing together breaks the usual order of agriculture and of ministry; others (Jacob, the prophets, the woman herself) had sown in Samaria.
9.question: Where are you reaping what others sowed, and where are you sowing for reapers you will never meet?

9.title: The Savior of the World
9.context: 'Savior of the world' is a title the Roman world used of emperors; here Samaritans give it to a Jewish teacher after two days in their town. Their confession also completes the pattern of this Gospel: belief outgrows the witness who started it.
9.question: The Samaritans moved from her words to hearing for themselves. Whose testimony started your faith, and what have you since heard for yourself?

10.title: A Prophet Has No Honor
10.context: Cana to Capernaum is roughly twenty miles, a hard day's walk for a desperate father. The official was likely a courtier of Herod Antipas, the ruler who would later mock Jesus at his trial in Luke's account.
10.question: The official's rank could not buy his son's life. Where has your own competence or standing run out, leaving only a request?

10.title: Unless You People See Signs
10.context: Jesus' rebuke is plural, aimed at a sign-hungry public, not only at this father. The official does not argue the point; his reply strips his prayer to its clock: come down before my child dies.
10.question: When Jesus' answer to your prayer begins with a rebuke, what do you do with the rebuke?

10.title: Go, Your Son Will Live
10.context: John marks the official's response as the hinge: he took Jesus at his word and departed. No arrangement for verification, no request for Jesus to come anyway; the word itself was treated as the deed.
10.question: What sentence of Jesus are you currently being asked to take at his word, with nothing to show for it yet?

10.title: The Very Hour
10.context: The seventh hour is about 1 p.m. The father's check of the hour is an investigator's move in a Gospel built on testimony; a distant healing is verified by timestamp, and the whole household believes.
10.question: Distance was nothing to the word spoken at Cana. How does that change the way you pray for people far from you?

10.title: The Second Sign
10.context: John's numbering of the signs (first at Cana, 2:11; second here, 4:54) frames the Galilean ministry between two Cana miracles, one at a wedding and one at a deathbed. Between them lies the whole pattern of his signs: glory revealed, faith answered.
10.question: John counts signs carefully. What are the numbered mercies, first, second, third, that you can count in your own story?

11.title: A Pool with Five Colonnades
11.context: Bethesda's twin pools and five porches were excavated north of the temple near the Sheep Gate, matching John's description. The verse about an angel stirring the water, found in later manuscripts, is not in the earliest copies or in the BSB text; the man's own words in verse 7 carry the belief.
11.question: Jesus asks a man disabled for thirty-eight years if he wants to get well. What long-standing condition in your life would you have to answer that question honestly?

11.title: Get Up, Pick Up Your Mat, and Walk
11.context: The man's answer names everyone else's advantage and his own helplessness, a theology of scarce healing. Jesus bypasses the pool entirely; the command carries its own strength, and 'immediately' is John's word for the result.
11.question: Where are you still explaining why healing cannot reach you, while Jesus is simply telling you to get up?

11.title: It Is Unlawful for You to Carry Your Mat
11.context: Carrying burdens was one of the labors later rabbinic tradition enumerated as forbidden on the Sabbath. The healed man's defense, 'the man who made me well told me,' is John's Gospel in miniature: obedience to the healer outranks the rulebook of the accusers.
11.question: The man did not even know his healer's name, yet he defended him. What has Jesus done for you that you could testify to before you understood it?

11.title: Stop Sinning, or Something Worse
11.context: The temple meeting is deliberate; Jesus finds the man. Interpreters differ over whether 'something worse' means a worse physical fate or the judgment of verse 29; the text leaves the warning hanging, and the man responds by reporting Jesus to the authorities.
11.question: Jesus' second word to the healed man is a warning, not a celebration. How do you receive follow-up words from God that are sterner than the first?

11.title: My Father Is at His Work, and I Too Am Working
11.context: Jewish theology itself granted that God works on the Sabbath, sustaining creation, without breaking it. Jesus' answer claims that exemption by sonship, and John states the authorities' conclusion plainly: this, not the mat, is why they sought to kill him.
11.question: John says the real charge was never the Sabbath but the claim 'God is my Father.' What claim of Jesus creates the sharpest tension in your world?

12.title: The Son Can Do Nothing by Himself
12.context: Jesus answers the equality charge with dependence: the Son imitates the Father the way an apprentice son in a family trade learned by watching. The claim is not distance from God but a unity of action that the discourse now unfolds.
12.question: Jesus describes his whole ministry as copying what he sees the Father do. What would change if you treated your days that way?

12.title: He Has Crossed Over from Death to Life
12.context: Resurrection and judgment, Israel's end-time hopes, are here reassigned to the Son and pulled into the present tense: the hearer 'has crossed over,' already. Verse 24 is one of the Gospel's strongest assurance statements.
12.question: What does it mean to you that eternal life, in verse 24, is something a believer has already crossed into?

12.title: All Who Are in Their Graves Will Hear His Voice
12.context: Verse 25 speaks of the dead hearing now ('the hour is coming and has now come'); verses 28-29 widen it to the general resurrection. 'Son of Man' reaches back to Daniel 7, where one like a son of man receives authority and judgment from the Ancient of Days.
12.question: Jesus speaks of two resurrections, life and judgment. How does that horizon change the weight of an ordinary day?

12.title: John Was a Lamp
12.context: Jesus conducts his defense like a trial, calling witnesses in order: the Baptist, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures. A lamp gives light but is not the light; the image gently returns the Baptist to his prologue role.
12.question: John was a lamp people enjoyed for a season. Whose temporary light helped you, and how do you honor it without mistaking it for the sun?

12.title: You Refuse to Come to Me to Have Life
12.context: 'Pore over' in verse 39 can be read as statement or command; either way the charge is that searching replaced coming. Moses as accuser (vv. 45-47) turns Israel's greatest advocate into the prosecution, a reversal the court audience would have felt sharply.
12.question: Is there an area where you study the Scriptures about something instead of coming to Jesus with it?

13.title: Where Can We Buy Bread?
13.context: John notes the Passover was near (v. 4), framing the feeding with Exodus associations the discourse will draw out: bread from heaven, a prophet like Moses. Philip, from nearby Bethsaida, is asked as the local; John tells us the question was a test.
13.question: Jesus asked Philip a question he already knew the answer to. What question is Jesus asking you as a test right now?

13.title: Five Barley Loaves and Two Small Fish
13.context: Two hundred denarii was roughly two hundred days' wages. Barley was the cheapest grain, the bread of the poor; Andrew's find is a child's packed lunch, and his question, 'what difference will these make,' is the arithmetic of scarcity speaking.
13.question: Andrew brought the little he found even while doubting its use. What small thing are you holding back because it looks like nothing among so many?

13.title: Gather the Pieces, So That Nothing Will Be Wasted
13.context: About five thousand men sat on the grass, a detail Mark's account also gives. The twelve baskets of leftovers, one per apostle, and the command against waste frame abundance with care rather than spectacle.
13.question: Jesus multiplied food and then collected leftovers. How do abundance and carefulness fit together in your handling of what God gives?

13.title: Make Him King by Force
13.context: 'The Prophet who is to come' is the Moses-like figure of Deuteronomy 18, expected at Passover season in a land under Rome. A bread king was exactly the Messiah the crowds wanted; Jesus withdraws rather than accept a crown from full stomachs.
13.question: Where are you tempted to give Jesus a role he refuses, king of your comfort rather than Lord of your life?

13.title: It Is I; Do Not Be Afraid
13.context: 'It is I' is the Greek ego eimi, the 'I am' that runs through this Gospel and echoes God's name in Exodus 3. The boat reaching the shore 'at once' (v. 21) is John's quiet second miracle inside the first.
13.question: In what storm has Jesus' 'It is I' been the whole sermon you needed?

14.title: You Ate the Loaves and Had Your Fill
14.context: The crowd's detective work about the boats is John's most logistical paragraph; their pursuit is genuine, and Jesus still names its motive: full stomachs. The seal of God (v. 27) was a mark of ownership and approval on the Son of Man.
14.question: Jesus distinguishes seeking him from seeking what he gives. How honest can you be about which one is driving your prayers lately?

14.title: The Work of God Is This: To Believe
14.context: The manna test is daring: Moses' sign lasted forty years and fed a nation daily. The crowd quotes Psalm 78:24, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat,' crediting Moses; Jesus' correction of the giver drives the discourse from here.
14.question: Where do you find yourself asking God for one more sign before you will believe what he has already said?

14.title: Give Us This Bread at All Times
14.context: Like the Samaritan woman's 'give me this water,' the request begins on the level of appetite and is answered on the level of a Person. The tense matters to John: the Father 'gives,' present and ongoing, where manna only 'was given.'
14.question: What would it mean for you to pray 'give us this bread at all times' and mean Jesus himself?

14.title: I Will Never Drive Away
14.context: This is the first of John's seven 'I am' sayings with a predicate: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. The Father's will in verses 39-40 is stated as loss-proof care: lose none, raise all, at the last day.
14.question: Jesus promises never to drive away anyone who comes. What fear of rejection does that promise answer in you?

14.title: Stop Grumbling Among Yourselves
14.context: 'Grumbling' is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's wilderness complaints against Moses. The Capernaum synagogue where this teaching happened has been excavated; its later limestone ruins stand over earlier basalt foundations from Jesus' century.
14.question: The crowd's objection was local knowledge: we know his parents. Where does familiarity with Jesus make you deaf to him?

15.title: How Can This Man Give Us His Flesh to Eat?
15.context: The saying was spoken in the Capernaum synagogue (v. 59). Readers have long debated how far the words point to the Lord's Supper, which John's Gospel never narrates; John lets the offense of the saying stand at full strength, and the union promised is mutual indwelling (v. 56).
15.question: Which of Jesus' hard sayings do you find yourself wanting to soften, and what might it cost to let it stand?

15.title: The Words I Have Spoken Are Spirit and Life
15.context: Even disciples, not only opponents, call the teaching difficult (Greek skleros, hard). Jesus' reply points past the flesh language to the ascension: what they will see when the Son of Man returns to where he was before.
15.question: When a teaching of Jesus offends you, what do you do with the offense: leave, argue, or stay and listen?

15.title: Do You Want to Leave Too?
15.context: Verse 66's number has often been noticed. The defection is of 'many of his disciples,' a wider circle than the Twelve, and Jesus' question to the Twelve leaves the door genuinely open; he will not hold followers by pressure.
15.question: Jesus let people walk away rather than dilute the word. How does that shape the way you hold your own convictions with people who leave?

15.title: To Whom Would We Go?
15.context: Peter's confession here, 'the Holy One of God,' comes at the ministry's lowest point in this Gospel, not at a triumph. John's note on Judas (v. 71) darkens it: the Twelve contain the betrayer from this moment in the reader's knowledge.
15.question: Peter stayed because there was nowhere else with words of eternal life. What has kept you with Jesus in a season when leaving was an option?

16.title: Show Yourself to the World
16.context: Tabernacles (Sukkot) was the autumn pilgrimage feast of booths, water, and lights, remembering the wilderness years. Jesus' brothers speak the language of publicity; verse 5's aside, that they did not believe, frames their advice as unbelief's strategy.
16.question: Family can love you and still not believe in you. How do you weigh advice from people who do not share your faith in what God is doing?

16.title: My Time Has Not Yet Come
16.context: Jesus distinguishes their time ('always at hand') from his 'time' governed by the Father, the same clock as the 'hour' of 2:4. He later goes up quietly; the feast crowds spend the week divided between 'good man' and 'deceiver,' whispering for fear of the authorities.
16.question: Where is your life being governed by God's timetable rather than other people's urgency?

16.title: How Did This Man Attain Such Learning?
16.context: Formal rabbinic training was the credential the temple establishment expected; Jesus' answer makes willingness to do God's will the doorway to recognizing true teaching (v. 17). The charge in verse 19, 'why are you trying to kill me,' sounds paranoid to a crowd unaware of the plot (cf. 5:18).
16.question: Jesus says doing God's will comes before knowing whether his teaching is from God. What step of obedience might unlock understanding you are waiting for?

16.title: Making the Whole Man Well on the Sabbath
16.context: Circumcision on the eighth day fell on the Sabbath regularly and was performed anyway, by the law's own priority. Jesus' 'whole man' argument contrasts a covenant cut on one member with a body made entirely well. The crowd's origin objection (v. 27) reflects a tradition that Messiah's origins would be hidden.
16.question: Where are you judging by outward appearances, in a person or a situation, instead of judging justly?

16.title: Streams of Living Water
16.context: On the feast's last day the priests poured water at the altar amid great ceremony, remembering the rock in the wilderness. Jesus' shout reassigns the water rite to himself and to believers. John adds that the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified, the cross before Pentecost.
16.question: Jesus makes his loudest invitation on the last and greatest day, to 'anyone' who is thirsty. What thirst in you is he addressing?

16.title: Never Has Anyone Spoken Like This Man
16.context: The officers' report is unique in ancient literature: an arrest party converted by the speech of its target. The leaders' Bethlehem objection (vv. 41-42) is dramatic irony; they do not know his birthplace. Their closing claim, that no prophet comes from Galilee, overlooks Jonah of Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25).
16.question: Nicodemus speaks one careful sentence of justice at personal cost. When has fairness required you to speak against your own side?

17.title: Each Went to His Own Home
17.context: The Mount of Olives, across the Kidron from the temple, is where Jesus regularly spent the nights of this final period (Luke 21:37). The account that follows, 7:53-8:11, is absent from the earliest surviving copies of John's Gospel and appears in different places in later ones; it stands in the BSB text where the church has long read it.
17.question: The council went home divided, and Jesus went to the mountain. Where do you go when a day of conflict ends?

17.title: Caught in the Act of Adultery
17.context: The law required both parties to an adultery to be judged (Leviticus 20:10), yet only the woman is produced, and John names the scene a test: accusing Jesus was the point. Roman rule also reserved executions to the governor, so either answer Jesus gave could be used against him.
17.question: The accusers used a person as evidence in an argument with Jesus. Where do you see people treated as exhibits today, and what is your part in it?

17.title: Let Him Who Is Without Sin Cast the First Stone
17.context: Deuteronomy 17 required the witnesses to throw the first stones of an execution, taking responsibility for the verdict. Jesus' sentence makes every volunteer witness examine himself first. What he wrote on the ground is the Gospel's only record of Jesus writing, and it is never disclosed.
17.question: The older accusers left first. What has age or experience taught you about your readiness to throw stones?

17.title: Neither Do I Condemn You
17.context: Jesus' two sentences hold what the whole Gospel holds: no condemnation (cf. 3:17) and a command to leave the sin behind. The woman is never named or followed up; the story's focus is the mercy that disarms judges and the word that sends the forgiven out changed.
17.question: Which of Jesus' two sentences do you most need to hear today: 'neither do I condemn you,' or 'go and sin no more'?

18.title: Your Testimony Is Not Valid
18.context: The scene is set near the temple treasury (v. 20), close to where the great lamps of Tabernacles had burned, giving 'light of the world' its setting. Jewish law required two witnesses in capital cases (Deuteronomy 19:15); Jesus claims the Father as his second witness.
18.question: Jesus answers a legal objection with knowledge of where he came from and where he is going. How settled are you about your own origin and destination in God?

18.title: When You Have Lifted Up the Son of Man
18.context: 'Lifted up' is John's double-edged word for the cross: hoisted up and exalted at once (3:14; 12:32). 'From above' and 'from below' are not geography but allegiance; verse 24's 'I am He' uses the same absolute 'I am' that climaxes in verse 58.
18.question: Jesus says people would know who he is by the lifting up. What has the cross taught you about Jesus that nothing else could?

18.title: The Truth Will Set You Free
18.context: The promise is addressed to believers who continue in his word, and it provokes the claim 'we have never been slaves to anyone,' a bold line from descendants of Egypt's slaves living under Rome. Jesus redefines slavery and freedom around sin and the Son's place in the house.
18.question: What does continuing in Jesus' word, not merely admiring it, look like in your ordinary week?

18.title: You Belong to Your Father, the Devil
18.context: The argument turns on paternity proven by practice: Abraham's works, God's love, or the devil's desires. The devil 'a murderer from the beginning' reaches back to Cain and the serpent; 'native language' of lies makes falsehood his mother tongue.
18.question: Jesus says actions, not ancestry, name our father. What do your recent actions say about whose family likeness you carry?

18.title: Before Abraham Was Born, I Am
18.context: The contrast of tenses is the claim: Abraham 'was born' (came into being); Jesus says 'I am,' the present tense of God's name in Exodus 3:14. The crowd's response, stones for blasphemy, shows they understood the claim exactly as he meant it.
18.question: Abraham rejoiced to see Jesus' day from centuries away. What are you rejoicing to see from a distance, by faith?

19.title: Who Sinned, This Man or His Parents?
19.context: The disciples' question reflects a common assumption that suffering traces to specific sin; Exodus 20:5's visiting of sins to children fed it. Jesus refuses the arithmetic entirely and replaces blame with purpose: the works of God displayed. The chapter performs the light saying of 8:12 and 9:5.
19.question: Where do you catch yourself doing the disciples' arithmetic over someone's suffering, or your own?

19.title: He Went and Washed and Came Back Seeing
19.context: Mud made with spit echoes the making of man from dust (Genesis 2:7) in an act of re-creation. Siloam, fed by the Gihon spring through Hezekiah's tunnel, means 'Sent,' as John notes; the man is sent to the pool as Jesus was sent into the world.
19.question: The man obeyed an instruction that looked undignified. What simple obedience stands between you and seeing something clearly?

19.title: He Is a Prophet
19.context: The Sabbath was again the tripwire (cf. ch. 5), and the council splits exactly as crowds have split all Gospel long. The healed man's rising estimate of Jesus is a thread to trace: a man called Jesus (v. 11), a prophet (v. 17), a worshiper God hears (v. 31), Lord (v. 38).
19.question: How has your own estimate of Jesus risen as you have seen what he does?

19.title: Ask Him. He Is Old Enough
19.context: Expulsion from the synagogue meant exclusion from worship, community, and livelihood; an agreement to impose it on confessors (v. 22) shows the conflict's stage. The parents' careful testimony protects themselves at their son's expense, a contrast John leaves the reader to feel.
19.question: Fear of being put outside the community silenced the parents. What fear most reliably silences your witness?

19.title: I Was Blind, but Now I See
19.context: 'Give glory to God' is a courtroom oath formula (Joshua 7:19) demanding confession, here demanding the court's version. The man's reply distinguishes what he does not know from the one thing he does, a model of testimony. His sermon to the council (vv. 30-33) is built entirely from their own premises.
19.question: What is your 'one thing I do know,' the experienced fact of Jesus that no argument can take from you?

19.title: Lord, I Believe
19.context: Jesus seeks the expelled man, as he sought the Samaritan woman in another register; 'Son of Man' is the title the man believed to. The closing exchange with the Pharisees states the chapter's reversal: sight claimed becomes guilt remaining.
19.question: The blind man ended worshiping; the seeing men ended blind. What does Jesus' 'do you believe' ask of you personally?

20.title: They Will Flee from a Stranger's Voice
20.context: Village sheepfolds held several flocks overnight under one gatekeeper; in the morning each shepherd called his own sheep out by voice. Jesus calls the picture a figure of speech (v. 6), and the Pharisees of chapter 9 are its first audience.
20.question: Sheep follow a voice they know and flee one they do not. Whose voices have the most practice at leading you, and how did they earn it?

20.title: I Have Come That They May Have Life in All Its Fullness
20.context: Gate and shepherd are two separate images in this chapter; Jesus claims both. 'In all its fullness' is the Greek perissos, abundance beyond necessity. The thief's three verbs, steal, kill, destroy, stand against the shepherd's one gift, life.
20.question: Where has Jesus' promised abundance shown up in your life in ways mere survival would never explain?

20.title: The Hired Hand Runs Away
20.context: Wolves were a real cost of Palestinian shepherding; hired hands were a known weak point, paid wages with no ownership in the flock. 'Good' here is the Greek kalos, beautiful or noble, the shepherd whose goodness is proven at the wolf.
20.question: Who has stayed with you at cost, like a shepherd rather than a hireling, and what did their staying teach you about Jesus?

20.title: I Lay Down My Life of My Own Accord
20.context: The mutual knowledge of shepherd and sheep is patterned on the Father and Son's (vv. 14-15). 'Other sheep not of this fold' looks beyond Israel, toward the Greeks of chapter 12 and the world of 3:16. Verse 18 insists the cross is voluntary at the deepest level.
20.question: Jesus says no one takes his life from him. How does a voluntary cross change the way you face what obedience may cost you?

20.title: Can a Demon Open the Eyes of the Blind?
20.context: Division (Greek schisma, a tear) is John's recurring verdict on Jesus' audiences (7:43; 9:16). The minority report rests on the blind man's healing, recent evidence from chapter 9 deployed in chapter 10's argument.
20.question: The crowd argued from a healed man's eyes. What evidence would you put on the table in an argument about who Jesus is?

21.title: If You Are the Christ, Tell Us Plainly
21.context: The Feast of Dedication is Hanukkah, marking the temple's rededication under Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC; it falls in winter, and Solomon's Colonnade was a roofed walkway on the temple's east side, sheltered from the cold.
21.question: The demand for plain speech came from people who had already rejected the works. What plain thing has Jesus said that you are still negotiating with?

21.title: No One Can Snatch Them Out of My Hand
21.context: Verses 28-29 place the sheep in two hands, the Son's and the Father's, and verse 30 explains the double grip: 'I and the Father are one.' The Greek 'one' is neuter, one thing or one work, not one person; the claim is unity of action and essence.
21.question: What fear does 'no one can snatch them' speak to most directly in your life right now?

21.title: For Which of These Do You Stone Me?
21.context: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). The accusers are unusually precise about the charge: not the works, but the claim, a man making himself God. In John's telling they state the Gospel's central question cleanly.
21.question: Jesus asks his accusers to name the work they stone him for. How do you handle it when the real objection to your faith is Jesus himself?

21.title: Believe the Works Themselves
21.context: Jesus argues from Psalm 82:6, where God calls Israel's judges 'gods,' reasoning from the lesser to the greater, a standard rabbinic move. His fallback offer, believe the works if not the words, has been his standing invitation since chapter 5.
21.question: If someone you love cannot yet believe Jesus' words, what works of his could you point them to without an argument?

21.title: Everything He Said About This Man Was True
21.context: Jesus withdraws to the Jordan wilderness where the Baptist began, beyond the reach of the temple authorities, and John's ministry comes full circle: no sign performed by the Baptist, yet his testimony is still gathering believers after his death.
21.question: John did no miracle, yet his witness outlived him. What testimony are you leaving that may bear fruit after you are gone?

22.title: Lord, the One You Love Is Sick
22.context: Bethany sat a little less than two miles east of Jerusalem, over the Mount of Olives. The sisters' message names no request; its address, 'the one you love,' does the asking. John identifies Mary ahead of time by the anointing she will perform in chapter 12.
22.question: The sisters sent facts and left the response to love. What situation in your life needs that kind of prayer?

22.title: He Stayed Where He Was for Two Days
22.context: Verse 4 pronounces the end at the beginning: glory, not death, will have the last word. The 'so' of verse 6, loved them, so he stayed, has troubled and comforted readers ever since; John insists the delay flows from love, not indifference.
22.question: When God's delay looks like absence, what do you hold onto: the explanation, or the love John insists is behind it?

22.title: Let Us Also Go, So That We May Die with Him
22.context: Twelve hours of daylight was the working day; the riddle says a man walking in his appointed light does not stumble. 'Fallen asleep' was a common figure for death (Daniel 12:2), and the misunderstanding pattern forces Jesus to speak plainly. Thomas's line is loyalty at its most pessimistic.
22.question: Thomas expected death and went anyway. What are you walking toward with Jesus while expecting the worst?

22.title: Lord, If You Had Been Here
22.context: Four days mattered: a popular belief held the soul lingered near the body three days, making the fourth day final. Martha goes out to meet Jesus while Mary stays with the mourners, true to their portraits in every Gospel. Her 'even now' (v. 22) holds faith and grief in one sentence.
22.question: Martha said 'if you had been here' and 'even now' in the same breath. Which of the two is your prayer today?

22.title: I Am the Resurrection and the Life
22.context: Martha's creed, resurrection at the last day, was mainstream Pharisaic hope (Daniel 12:2). Jesus relocates the hope from a day to a person standing in front of her. Her confession in verse 27 matches the Gospel's purpose statement (20:31) almost word for word.
22.question: Jesus asks Martha 'do you believe this' at a tomb, before any miracle. What do you believe before you have seen the outcome?

23.title: The Teacher Is Here and Is Asking for You
23.context: Martha's whisper to Mary is the only errand she runs in the chapter, and it moves the mourners like a procession. Mary's sentence repeats Martha's exactly (v. 21), showing the sisters had rehearsed their grief together. His being 'deeply moved' carries an edge of indignation at death itself.
23.question: Mary fell at his feet with the same words as her sister. When grief repeats itself in your house, what do you bring to Jesus' feet?

23.title: Jesus Wept
23.context: Verse 35 is the shortest verse in English Bibles. The Greek verb suggests quiet tears, distinct from the loud mourning around him. The bystanders read the tears two ways, love or helplessness, the crowd's usual two verdicts on Jesus.
23.question: Jesus wept knowing he was about to raise Lazarus. What does that teach you about tears that are not unbelief?

23.title: Lord, by Now He Stinks
23.context: Tombs of the period were caves or rock-cut chambers sealed by a rolling or laid stone. Martha's protest is practical and exact: four days of decay in that climate. Jesus answers with the promise of verse 4, glory to be seen by believing first.
23.question: Martha believed and still protested at the stone. Where do you believe and protest at the same time?

23.title: Lazarus, Come Out!
23.context: The prayer is spoken aloud 'for the benefit of the people standing here,' so the crowd will credit the Sender. The loud voice echoes 5:28, the voice all in the graves will hear. Grave clothes unwound by the mourners make the community participants in the miracle's last step.
23.question: Jesus gave the bystanders the finishing work, 'unwrap him and let him go.' Who might need you to help unwrap what God has raised?

23.title: One Man Die for the People
23.context: Caiaphas, high priest for eighteen years by political survival, speaks realpolitik; John reads prophecy in it God did not ask his permission for (vv. 51-52). The council's fear, losing 'our place and our nation' to Rome, came true in AD 70 by the opposite road. Ephraim, Jesus' withdrawal town, lay north of Jerusalem near the wilderness.
23.question: Caiaphas meant his words cynically and God meant them truly. Where have you seen God overrule the meaning of someone's words or plans?

24.title: Martha Served, and Lazarus Reclined at the Table
24.context: Six days before the Passover sets the week's clock; the dinner at Bethany is the calm before it. The guest list itself is testimony: a host family marked by death, and its dead man eating. Matthew and Mark tell a similar anointing at Simon the leper's house; John's details here are his own.
24.question: Lazarus ate dinner as evidence. What ordinary activity in your life is itself a testimony to what Jesus has done?

24.title: The House Was Filled with the Fragrance
24.context: Nard was an imported Himalayan root perfume; three hundred denarii was about a year's wages for a laborer. Anointing feet, and wiping them with unbound hair, was servanthood past the edge of propriety. John's note on Judas and the money bag (v. 6) is his Gospel's explanation of a motive.
24.question: Mary's worship was extravagant and criticized as waste. What act of devotion have you been tempted to price instead of offer?

24.title: She Has Kept This for the Day of My Burial
24.context: Jesus reads Mary's act prophetically: burial preparation for a body that would not get its full burial rites in time on Friday. 'The poor you will always have with you' quotes Deuteronomy 15:11, a passage about openhanded generosity, not an excuse for neglect.
24.question: Mary understood the week better than the treasurer did. What do you sense about Jesus' path that people counting costs around you may be missing?

24.title: Plans to Kill Lazarus as Well
24.context: The plot against Lazarus is John's alone, and its logic is the council's arithmetic perfected: evidence of life must die because it is believed. 'Deserting them' (v. 11) shows the issue was allegiance hemorrhaging, not theology in the abstract.
24.question: The council targeted the evidence, not only the argument. What evidence of Jesus in your life is hardest for skeptics to explain away?

24.title: Blessed Is the King of Israel
24.context: Palm branches were national symbols, stamped on Jewish coins and waved for conquering heroes since the Maccabees. The donkey quote is Zechariah 9:9, a king coming in peace; verse 16 admits the disciples only connected the pieces after the resurrection.
24.question: The crowds wanted a king on their terms. How do you welcome Jesus when his kingship takes a donkey's road instead of a warhorse's?

25.title: Sir, We Want to See Jesus
25.context: Greeks here are likely God-fearing Gentiles who worshiped at the feasts without full conversion. They approach Philip, whose Greek name and Bethsaida background made him a natural door. Jesus' answer, that the hour has come (v. 23), reverses every 'not yet' since 2:4; the world's arrival starts the clock.
25.question: The Greeks' request reached Jesus through two intermediaries. Who might be asking for Jesus through you, politely and indirectly?

25.title: Unless a Kernel of Wheat Falls
25.context: The seed parable makes multiplication run through burial. Verse 27's troubled soul and refused rescue prayer are John's counterpart to Gethsemane, spoken publicly. The voice from heaven is this Gospel's third audible heaven, after the Baptist's testimony and before no other; the crowd hears thunder or an angel.
25.question: Jesus says fruitfulness requires the seed to die. What in your life is being asked to fall into the ground?

25.title: Now the Prince of This World Will Be Cast Out
25.context: John explains 'lifted up' himself in verse 33: it indicates the kind of death. The crowd's objection, that the Christ remains forever (from passages like Psalm 89 and Daniel 7), shows careful Bible readers tripping over the cross. His final public word in this Gospel is walk in the light while you have it.
25.question: Jesus calls the cross a casting out of the world's prince and a drawing of all people. How do you see the cross doing both at once?

25.title: They Loved Praise from Men
25.context: John quotes Isaiah twice: 53:1 on unbelief and 6:10 on hardening, then says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory (v. 41). The secret believers of verse 42, leaders who feared expulsion, are Nicodemus's company; verse 43 diagnoses them in one line about praise.
25.question: Verse 43 says the secret believers loved praise from men more than praise from God. Where does that love most threaten your own confession?

25.title: Whoever Sees Me Sees the One Who Sent Me
25.context: These verses are a summary cry, gathering the Gospel's themes: belief, seeing, light, not judging but saving, and the word as future judge. That Jesus 'cried out' (v. 44) after hiding himself (v. 36) makes the passage his farewell address to the public.
25.question: Jesus' last public words return to the Sender. What one sentence of his would you choose as the summary a stranger should hear first?

26.title: He Loved Them to the Very End
26.context: 'To the very end' is also 'to the uttermost'; the Greek carries both the time and the degree. This verse is the doorway into the farewell discourse (chs. 13-17), the longest sustained teaching in the Gospels, given to the eleven alone.
26.question: The whole farewell happens under the heading of love to the end. How does that heading change the way you hear commands that follow it?

26.title: He Began to Wash the Disciples' Feet
26.context: Foot washing was slave's work, done by the lowest servant or by guests themselves from a provided basin; a teacher doing it for students inverted the house. Peter's 'never' and then 'not only my feet' are his two speeds, refusal and excess, with Jesus correcting both.
26.question: Jesus washes feet with full knowledge of who he is (v. 3). How does security about your identity free you to serve low?

26.title: I Have Set You an Example
26.context: The interpretation is given by Jesus himself: this was example, not only symbol. Verse 18 quotes Psalm 41:9, a friend at the table lifting his heel, David's Ahithophel story replayed with Judas. The blessing is located in doing (v. 17), not in knowing.
26.question: Jesus locates the blessing in the doing, not the knowing. What known thing is waiting on your doing?

26.title: One of You Will Betray Me
26.context: Sharing a dipped morsel was a host's gesture of honor, which makes the sign's kindness part of its horror. The disciple whom Jesus loved appears here for the first time under that title; John never names him. 'It was night' (v. 30) closes the exit with the Gospel's whole imagery in two words.
26.question: Jesus gave his betrayer the morsel of honor and washed his feet. What does his conduct toward Judas ask of the way you treat people you cannot trust?

26.title: Love One Another, As I Have Loved You
26.context: The new commandment's newness is its measure: 'as I have loved you,' spoken with the towel and the cross in view. 'Little children' is an address Jesus uses only here in this Gospel. Peter's vow and its answer set the night's second clock, the rooster, beside the hour.
26.question: The badge Jesus chose for his disciples is mutual love, not knowledge or power. How visible is that badge in your community right now?

27.title: In My Father's House Are Many Rooms
27.context: 'Rooms' (monai) shares its root with the verb 'remain' that fills chapter 15; the house image is about abiding, not real estate. 'Prepare a place' is the pioneer's errand, and verse 3 promises the return that the rest of the New Testament takes up.
27.question: Jesus frames his leaving as preparing and his absence as temporary. How does that frame change the way you wait for him?

27.title: I Am the Way and the Truth and the Life
27.context: Thomas's literal question draws the Gospel's most exclusive saying. 'Way' had a long life ahead of it: the first believers were called followers of the Way (Acts 9:2). The saying answers where he is going (to the Father) with who he is.
27.question: Thomas asked because he admitted he did not know. What question are you not asking Jesus because it would expose how lost you feel?

27.title: Anyone Who Has Seen Me Has Seen the Father
27.context: Philip's request echoes Moses' 'show me your glory' (Exodus 33:18). The greater works of verse 12 are tied to Jesus' going to the Father and to prayer in his name, and the church's worldwide witness in Acts is usually seen as their first installment.
27.question: Philip wanted one more vision; Jesus pointed at three years of knowing him. What have you already seen of the Father in Jesus that you undervalue?

27.title: Another Advocate to Be with You Forever
27.context: Advocate renders parakletos, one called alongside, a helper, intercessor, or defense counsel. 'Another' implies Jesus was the first (1 John 2:1 calls him our advocate with the Father). Orphans in verse 18 is the exact fear of men about to lose their master.
27.question: Jesus promises presence, not explanations, to men facing loss. Where do you need his 'I will not leave you as orphans' today?

27.title: Peace I Leave with You
27.context: Judas, not Iscariot, is Thaddaeus of the other lists; John pauses to distinguish him at the night's most tender point. The Spirit's reminding work (v. 26) is John's own account of how this Gospel came to be written accurately decades later. Peace (shalom) here is a bequest, left like property in a will.
27.question: Jesus left his peace as an inheritance the night before his death. What part of that bequest are you living on, and what part is unclaimed?

27.title: The Prince of This World Has No Claim on Me
27.context: 'The Father is greater than I' (v. 28) has been debated for centuries; in context it explains why the disciples should rejoice at his return to the Father, within the mission the Father sent. 'Get up, let us go' (v. 31) ends the room discourse, though chapters 15-17 continue the talk on the way or at the garden's edge.
27.question: Jesus told them everything in advance 'so that you will believe.' What has Jesus told you in advance that you are meant to remember in a hard hour?

28.title: I Am the True Vine
28.context: Israel was God's vine in Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5, and a golden vine adorned the temple front; 'true' sets Jesus as the reality those images pointed to. Pruning (the Greek also means cleansing) ties the knife to the word already spoken in verse 3.
28.question: Pruning is care aimed at fruit, not punishment. Where might the Father's knife in your life be vineyard work rather than rejection?

28.title: Apart from Me You Can Do Nothing
28.context: 'Remain' (meno) is used ten times in verses 4-10, the chapter's heartbeat. Fruit here is the Gospel's broad word for a life that reproduces the vine's life: love, obedience, answered prayer, and witness, not a single metric.
28.question: What are you attempting right now at a pace or in a way that has quietly detached from the vine?

28.title: No Longer Do I Call You Servants
28.context: Friend of the king was a court title in the ancient world, an insider with access; Jesus grounds it in disclosure, everything made known. Verse 16 reverses the custom by which students chose their rabbi; here the rabbi chose, and appointed, with fruit that remains as the assignment.
28.question: Jesus calls you friend and tells you his business. How does friendship with him differ from the servanthood you sometimes slip back into?

28.title: They Hated Me Without Reason
28.context: The hatred theme completes the farewell's realism: chosen out of the world means treated like the One the world rejected. The quotation is Psalm 35:19 or 69:4, both psalms of the righteous sufferer, quoted as 'their Law' fulfilled by the hatred itself.
28.question: Jesus forecasts hatred so his followers will not read it as failure. How does that forecast steady you when faithfulness costs you socially?

28.title: He Will Testify About Me
28.context: Verse 26's 'proceeds from the Father' became one of the most contested phrases in church history between East and West. In context its work is simpler: the Spirit testifies about Jesus, and the apostles' qualification for testifying is that they were there 'from the beginning.'
28.question: Your qualification to testify, like theirs, is having been with Jesus. What have you been with him through that qualifies your witness?

29.title: They Will Expel You from the Synagogue
29.context: Expulsion from the synagogue is the threat already operating in chapters 9 and 12; here it escalates to killing offered as worship. Jesus' stated reason for the warnings is memory: when the hour comes, they will remember he told them, and not fall away.
29.question: What warning of Jesus, remembered at the right hour, has kept you standing?

29.title: It Is for Your Good That I Am Going Away
29.context: None of them asks where he is going now; grief has filled the question-asking part of them. The Helper's courtroom work (vv. 8-11) convicts the world on three counts: sin defined by unbelief, righteousness vindicated by Jesus' return to the Father, and judgment sealed at the cross.
29.question: Jesus calls his leaving 'for your good.' What good has only become visible to you after a loss you would not have chosen?

29.title: The Spirit of Truth Will Guide You
29.context: 'I still have much to tell you, but you cannot bear it now' sets a mercy rule for revelation: truth on God's schedule. The Spirit's self-effacing pattern, he will not speak on his own, mirrors the Son's (5:19), and his subject is always Jesus.
29.question: Jesus says some truth waits until we can bear it. What are you trusting him to show you in his timing rather than yours?

29.title: A Little While, and You Will See Me
29.context: The 'little while' saying puzzles the disciples in the room the way it puzzles readers; the childbirth image answers it, pain real, brief, and forgotten into joy. Verse 24 introduces the new era of asking the Father in Jesus' name, with fullness of joy as its promised atmosphere.
29.question: Jesus compares his friends' grief to labor, real pain with a person at the end of it. What grief of yours is he asking you to read that way?

29.title: The Father Himself Loves You
29.context: 'Figures of speech' will give way to plain speech, and the first plain sentence in the passage is about the Father's own love, not a relay through Jesus as gatekeeper. The creed of verse 28 compresses the Gospel: from the Father, into the world, out of the world, back to the Father.
29.question: Jesus says the Father himself loves you, directly. How does that sentence re-order your picture of prayer?

29.title: You Will Be Scattered, Each to His Own Home
29.context: Their confession of verse 30 is sincere and shallow at once; within hours it scatters. Jesus' closing line is spoken in the past tense about a victory not yet visibly won ('I have overcome'), and it is John's last word of the farewell before the prayer.
29.question: Jesus promises peace located in him, in a world he guarantees will hold trouble. Where do you go looking for peace 'in me' rather than in changed circumstances?

30.title: Father, the Hour Has Come
30.context: Chapter 17 is called the High Priestly Prayer, Jesus interceding as he is about to offer himself. Verse 3 defines eternal life as knowledge, relational, not merely duration. The prayer opens with mutual glorification and finished work spoken before the cross, in the same past tense as 16:33.
30.question: How does verse 3's definition of eternal life, knowing God, change what you think you are asking for when you pray for it?

30.title: I Have Revealed Your Name
30.context: Jesus reports to the Father like a steward rendering an account: the men given, the words given, the belief given back. 'They have obeyed your word' (v. 6) is a generous assessment of the eleven on the night they will scatter; grace describes them by their faith, not their imminent failure.
30.question: Jesus describes his disciples to the Father more generously than their record reads. What does that suggest about how he describes you?

30.title: I Am Not Praying for the World
30.context: The restriction of verse 9 is about this prayer's errand, these men as the seed of the church, not about God's love for the world (3:16). 'Holy Father, protect them' (v. 11) is the only place Jesus addresses the Father as Holy, and protection by the name is protection by belonging.
30.question: Jesus prayed protection for his friends' unity as specifically as for their safety. Who needs you to pray that way for their oneness?

30.title: Sanctify Them by the Truth
30.context: Sanctify means set apart for God's use; Jesus asks for it 'by the truth' and identifies the truth as God's word. 'I sanctify myself' (v. 19) is priestly language: the offerer consecrates himself as the offering, for their sakes, which frames the cross as an act of consecration, not defeat.
30.question: Being 'in the world' but not 'of it' is the pattern here. Where is that balance hardest for you to hold?

30.title: That All of Them May Be One
30.context: The prayer's last reach is everyone who will ever believe through the apostles' message, which includes every reader since. Its petition is unity patterned on the Trinity, with a stated missionary purpose, 'so that the world may believe,' and its end is the glory given and shared (v. 22).
30.question: You are named in this prayer, one of those who believe through their message. What does it mean to you that Jesus prayed for your unity with other believers that night?

31.title: A Detachment of Soldiers and Officials of the Jews
31.context: Kidron is a winter torrent valley between the city and the garden on the Mount of Olives. 'Detachment' translates the Greek speira, a cohort; John's readers would hear Roman weight in the word, though the arrest party was likely temple police with Roman backing. Lanterns at Passover moon means portable light, carried by men about to meet the light of the world.
31.question: John says Jesus frequented this garden, and so did his betrayer. What do you make of Jesus keeping his habits when he knew they made him findable?

31.title: I Am He
31.context: Stepping forward and asking the questions is Gethsemane inverted: the sought man seeks the seekers. 'I am he' carries the absolute 'I am' of chapter 8; the soldiers falling backward at it is John's single flash of the glory in the arrest. Verse 9 treats his own 17:12 prayer as Scripture fulfilled.
31.question: Jesus protects the sheep while surrendering himself. Where have you seen him keep you safe in the middle of something he did not spare himself?

31.title: Put Your Sword Away
31.context: John names the swordsman (Peter) and the wounded man (Malchus), details the other accounts leave anonymous; the high priest's servant loses and, in Luke's account, regains his ear. 'The cup the Father has given me' is the prayer of the other Gospels' garden rendered as a settled fact in this one.
31.question: Peter defended Jesus with the wrong weapon at the wrong hour. When has your defense of a good cause needed Jesus to tell you to put it away?

31.title: I Will Follow You
31.context: The other disciple's access gets Peter inside the courtyard and into range of the girl at the door. Her question ('You are not one of his disciples, are you?') expects the answer no, which is the answer she gets. The charcoal fire (anthrakia) appears only twice in the New Testament, here and at the restoration breakfast of chapter 21.
31.question: Peter's first denial was to the least powerful person in the scene. Where do small-audience moments test your allegiance most?

31.title: Ask Those Who Heard Me
31.context: The hearing before Annas, the former high priest and Caiaphas's father-in-law, was irregular, at night and in private. Jesus' reply, that he taught openly in synagogue and temple, is a legal answer: witnesses exist; call them. The blow from the officer and Jesus' calm demand for evidence mirror Paul's hearing in Acts 23.
31.question: Jesus answered an illegal blow by demanding evidence of wrongdoing. How do you answer mistreatment without returning it or bending the truth?

31.title: The Rooster Crowed
31.context: John interleaves the denials with the hearing inside, so Peter warms himself while Jesus is struck. The second questioner is a servant of the high priest, a relative of Malchus, and his evidence is eyewitness: the garden. The denial and the crow land in the same verse, with no comment from the evangelist.
31.question: John records the crowing without commentary, as if the sound explains itself. What sound or moment has marked a failure you will never forget?

32.title: No Power to Release or Crucify
32.context: The Praetorium was the governor's Jerusalem residence, likely Herod's palace. The accusers' scruple about entering a Gentile house at Passover (v. 28) sits beside their errand, which John leaves the reader to weigh. 'Not lawful for us to put anyone to death' confirms Roman reservation of capital sentences.
32.question: The accusers protected their ritual cleanness on the way to demand an execution. Where can religious carefulness coexist with injustice in your own habits?

32.title: My Kingdom Is Not of This World
32.context: Pilate's first question expects the sedition charge; Jesus' answer defines kingship by origin and method, truth rather than armies. 'You say rightly' in other translations aside, the BSB's 'You say that I am a king' accepts the title on his own terms: born and come into the world to testify to the truth.
32.question: Jesus ties his kingship to witnessing to the truth rather than to force. What does that kingship look like when you submit an area of your life to it?

32.title: What Is Truth?
32.context: Pilate's question has been read as cynical, weary, or sincere for two thousand years; John records that he asked it and left without waiting for the answer. Barabbas was a bandit or insurrectionist; the crowd's choice between him and Jesus is the trial's bitter exchange, a guilty man released by custom as the innocent is condemned.
32.question: Pilate asked the right question and walked out on the answer. What question have you asked God and then not stayed to hear out?

32.title: Hail, King of the Jews!
32.context: Flogging (mastigoo) was a Roman scourging that could itself be lethal. The crown of thorns and purple robe were soldiers' mock coronation gear. 'Here is the man' (ecce homo in the Latin tradition) is Pilate's attempt at pity as policy; it failed when the chief priests answered with the law charge of verse 7.
32.question: Pilate presented Jesus as an object of pity; the priests answered with a theological charge. Which response to Jesus is more dangerous in your view, contempt or doctrine used as a weapon?

32.title: Where Do You Come From?
32.context: Pilate's fear (v. 8) is a Roman's fear of the numinous; his question about origin is the Gospel's own question (7:27; 8:14). Verse 11 grants responsibility's order: Pilate's borrowed authority beneath God's, and the greater sin assigned to the one who handed Jesus over.
32.question: Jesus tells Pilate his authority is borrowed from above. How does that sentence change the way you face human authority that frightens you?

32.title: We Have No King but Caesar
32.context: Gabbatha, the Stone Pavement, marks the judgment seat outdoors. The sixth hour here is a known puzzle against Mark's third hour for the crucifixion; reckonings differ (Roman from midnight, Jewish from dawn). 'Friend of Caesar' (v. 12) was a title and a threat; the priests' final line repudiates the theocracy of 1 Samuel 8 to secure a death.
32.question: The priests chose Caesar over their Messiah to win one verdict. What lesser loyalty have you been tempted to swear to, just to settle something now?

33.title: He Carried His Own Cross
33.context: John omits Simon of Cyrene; in this telling Jesus bears the cross out himself, as the Father's Son bearing the wood like Isaac's in Genesis 22. Golgotha, Place of the Skull, sat outside the city wall by a road. The trilingual sign was Rome's public notice of the charge, and the priests' protest about its wording is their last appearance at the cross.
33.question: John shows Jesus carrying his own cross out of the city. What burden in this chapter of your life is he carrying that you have been picturing yourself under alone?

33.title: They Cast Lots for My Clothing
33.context: A crucifixion detail squad was four soldiers, a quaternion, matching the four shares. The seamless tunic was woven in one piece from the top, valuable enough to gamble rather than tear. John quotes Psalm 22:18 and marks the fulfillment himself; the soldiers act as unwitting scribes of Scripture.
33.question: The soldiers gambled under the cross for a seamless robe. What does the contrast between their business and his suffering expose about ordinary indifference?

33.title: Woman, Here Is Your Son
33.context: The women at the cross include, by John's list, his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Providing for his mother from the cross, by entrusting her to the beloved disciple, is this Gospel's only act of family business at the crucifixion. 'From that hour' the disciple took her into his home.
33.question: In his worst hour Jesus arranged his mother's care. What responsibility of love is he asking you not to drop under pressure?

33.title: It Is Finished
33.context: 'I am thirsty' fulfills Psalm 69:21; hyssop was the small brush used at the first Passover to paint the doorposts with blood (Exodus 12:22). 'It is finished' (tetelestai) is a single Greek word used of debts paid in full and work completed. He 'gave up his spirit,' John's wording for a death handed over, not taken.
33.question: Jesus' last word in this Gospel is completion, not complaint. What work in your life needs to reach a 'finished' you can hand over, instead of an abandoned one?

33.title: Not One of His Bones Will Be Broken
33.context: Breaking the legs (crurifragium) hastened death by suffocation before the Sabbath, doubly urgent at Passover. The spear thrust and the flow of blood and water are given an eyewitness pledge (v. 35), the beloved disciple's courtroom signature on the physical fact of the death. The Scriptures quoted are Exodus 12:46 (the Passover lamb) and Zechariah 12:10.
33.question: John stakes his testimony on having watched the spear go in. Why does the physical reality of Jesus' death matter to your faith?

33.title: A Garden Tomb Where No One Had Ever Been Laid
33.context: Joseph of Arimathea's secrecy ('for fear of the Jews') matches Nicodemus coming 'at night,' and both men step into the open at the burial. Seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes is a royal quantity, like the burial spices of King Asa (2 Chronicles 16:14). John's garden setting frames the story: arrest in a garden, burial in a garden, and a gardener mistaken on Sunday.
33.question: Two secret disciples became public at the burial, when it cost the most. What conviction of yours is waiting for its expensive moment?

34.title: We Do Not Know Where They Have Put Him
34.context: Mary Magdalene heads the witness list in all four Gospels. The removed stone was the large disk rolled across the tomb's entrance. Her report's 'we' (v. 2) implies companions the other accounts name; John's camera stays on Mary alone.
34.question: Mary's first interpretation of the empty tomb was theft. What loss in your life might have a resurrection explanation you have not considered yet?

34.title: He Saw and Believed
34.context: The beloved disciple outruns Peter but stops at the entrance; Peter enters first. The head cloth 'rolled up' in its own place is the detail on which the belief of verse 8 turns: grave robbers do not fold. Verse 9 admits the belief ran ahead of their Scripture understanding, not behind it.
34.question: The beloved disciple believed from evidence arranged in an empty tomb. What ordered evidence of God's work is in front of you right now?

34.title: Woman, Why Are You Weeping?
34.context: Angels sit where the body lay, at head and feet, a picture many readers hear against the cherubim over the ark's mercy seat. Mary's failure to recognize Jesus repeats the Emmaus pattern in Luke; grief and the unexpected form Jesus takes both figure in it.
34.question: Mary spoke to Jesus without knowing it was him. When have you discovered later that he was in a conversation you thought was ordinary?

34.title: Mary
34.context: Rabboni is Aramaic for 'my teacher,' a more personal form than Rabbi. 'Do not cling to me' marks a changed mode of presence, not a rejection; the message she carries renames the disciples 'my brothers' for the first time in this Gospel, and her 'I have seen the Lord' is the resurrection's first sermon.
34.question: Jesus called Mary by name out of her grief. What is he calling you by name out of, today?

34.title: As the Father Has Sent Me, I Am Sending You
34.context: The locked doors are stated twice (vv. 19, 26) as the room's condition; faith's fears are physical here. The breathing on them echoes Genesis 2:7 and Ezekiel 37, God's breath making life. The forgiveness authority of verse 23 is given to the gathered disciples as a body.
34.question: Jesus' first word to men who had abandoned him was 'peace.' How does he usually greet you after a failure?

34.title: My Lord and My God
34.context: Thomas's conditions reverse the report he refused: nail marks, finger, hand in the side. Jesus offers exactly the evidence demanded, and Thomas's answer gives the Gospel its climactic confession, answering the prologue's 'the Word was God' (1:1). The beatitude of verse 29 turns from Thomas to every later reader.
34.question: Thomas's doubt ended in the fullest confession in the book. What condition have you set for belief that Jesus might be waiting to meet and then move you past?

34.title: These Are Written That You May Believe
34.context: This is the Gospel's purpose statement, its own colophon, and it addresses the reader directly: belief, and life in his name, are the book's intended effects. Chapter 21 follows as an epilogue the book itself seems to add after its ending, like a postscript the author could not leave unwritten.
34.question: John says he wrote so that you may believe and have life. What has this Gospel, read closely, actually produced in you?

35.title: I Am Going Fishing
35.context: The Sea of Tiberias is the Gospel's other name for the Sea of Galilee (6:1). The seven named and unnamed disciples gather where Jesus first called several of them. An all-night empty catch on their home water sets the stage for a stranger's instruction.
35.question: After the resurrection, Peter went back to the nets. What old work do you return to when you are waiting for instructions?

35.title: Cast the Net on the Right Side
35.context: Recognition follows the pattern again: the beloved disciple sees first ('It is the Lord'), and Peter acts first, into the water. A hundred yards is close enough to shout; the scene measures everything the way fishermen do.
35.question: Peter jumped in the moment he knew. What is the difference between your recognition of Jesus and your movement toward him?

35.title: Come, Have Breakfast
35.context: A charcoal fire links this beach to the courtyard of the denials (18:18), the only two charcoal fires in the New Testament. One hundred fifty-three large fish is a fisherman's exact count; interpreters have proposed symbolisms for centuries, but John simply records the number and the unbroken net.
35.question: Jesus had breakfast ready before he asked Peter anything. What does his order, feed first, restore second, teach you about how he handles your failures?

35.title: Do You Love Me More Than These?
35.context: Jesus asks by Peter's birth name, Simon son of John, three times, matching the three denials beside the other fire. The commission shifts each time: feed my lambs, shepherd my sheep, feed my sheep. The Greek varies between two words for love and two for knowing; Peter's grief at the third asking is recorded as plainly as his answers.
35.question: Peter's restoration was a job, not a lecture. What work has Jesus handed you as the way forward from a failure?

35.title: You Follow Me
35.context: Stretching out the hands was an early church picture of crucifixion, and John's aside says the saying foretold the death by which Peter would glorify God. The correction of Peter's comparison is the last command of the book: your road is yours; his is not yours to audit.
35.question: Jesus refuses Peter's 'what about him?' Where is a comparison with someone else's road distracting you from simply following?

35.title: The World Itself Could Not Contain the Books
35.context: The rumor about the beloved disciple (vv. 22-23) is the book's one correction of its own readers, delivered by the community voice, 'we know that his testimony is true.' Verse 25's hyperbole closes the Gospel that opened with eternity: the subject overflows the format.
35.question: The Gospel ends confessing it could not contain its subject. What has Jesus done in your life that no retelling of yours will ever fully hold?
